passage: In the Class 10 physics lab, Vidya ma'am was explaining why both bulbs in a parallel circuit stayed bright. Raghav leaned back on his stool. "Ma'am, that's not fully right," he said. "I watched a series on electricity. Current is basically like water, so the second bulb should be dimmer." A few students turned. Vidya ma'am handed him the wires. "Show us." Raghav connected them confidently, flipped the switch, and both bulbs glowed equally bright. He stared. "Maybe the battery's wrong." "Try another." Same result. "The videos were really detailed," he muttered, pulling at his sleeve. Ma'am smiled. "Water is a helpful picture. It just has limits you haven't met yet."

qa.q: What happened when Raghav flipped the switch?
qa.a: Both bulbs glowed equally bright.

qa.q: Why did Raghav feel confident enough to correct the teacher?
qa.a: A video series gave him a neat picture, water in pipes, and it felt complete; he didn't yet know enough to see where the picture breaks down.

qa.q: What could Raghav do after this lab?
qa.a: He could ask where the water picture stops working and read the chapter alongside the videos, treating what he learned as a start rather than expertise.

qa.q: How might Vidya ma'am see Raghav's challenge?
qa.a: She seems to see keen curiosity with a gap, not rudeness, so she lets the experiment show him instead of scolding him.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy who, after a few videos, thinks he knows the topic better than his teacher and cannot yet see what he is missing.

passage:
Hi Leela didi,
Big news: I now understand black holes better than our physics sir. I watched six videos this week, and one was two hours long! Today in class sir said nothing can escape a black hole, and I told him that's outdated, because black holes leak something at the edge. He asked me to explain how. I said it's because of quantum stuff. He asked what "quantum stuff" meant. I said it's complicated. Everyone laughed, but honestly I think he just didn't know. Anyway, you're doing astrophysics, so you'll agree with me, right? Maybe I'll skip his class and learn it all online.
Your little brother,
Chetan

qa.q: How many videos did Chetan watch this week?
qa.a: Chetan watched six videos this week.

qa.q: Why does Chetan believe he understands black holes better than his physics sir?
qa.a: Six videos gave him exciting ideas and words, so he feels expert; he doesn't yet know enough to notice he can't explain them.

qa.q: What could Leela didi write back to help Chetan?
qa.a: She could praise his interest and ask him to explain the leaking idea step by step; where he gets stuck will show him what the videos skipped.

qa.q: How might the physics sir have felt during the exchange?
qa.a: Sir probably felt patient but concerned, asking questions to help Chetan see the gap rather than shutting him down.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy who, after a few videos, believes he knows more than his teacher and cannot see what he is missing.

passage: Damini, listen. Tanvir here has cracked coding. Seriously. I watched maybe five videos last weekend and built a calculator. A calculator! Our computer teacher spends three weeks on loops. Three weeks! I learned them in twenty minutes. Today I told him his method is old-fashioned and he should just show the videos. He asked me to add error handling to my calculator. I said it doesn't need any, it works. He typed a letter instead of a number and the whole thing crashed. Okay, fine, that's a small thing. Honestly, I think teachers make it sound harder than it is so they have something to teach. Next month I'll build a whole app.

qa.q: What did the teacher type that made the calculator crash?
qa.a: He typed a letter instead of a number and the whole thing crashed.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir think teachers make coding sound harder than it is?
qa.a: Building one calculator after a few videos felt like mastery, so Tanvir can't yet see how much is missing, and the crash seems small rather than a sign of the gap.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanvir after the crash?
qa.a: Treat the crash as a clue: ask the teacher what error handling covers, try breaking the calculator on purpose, and notice how much there is still to learn.

qa.q: How might Damini hear this?
qa.a: Damini may enjoy the excitement but also notice the crash being brushed aside, and wonder whether Tanvir is ready to build a whole app.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after a few videos, believes they know coding better than the teacher and cannot see the gaps.

passage: I'm Siddharth, and I sit behind Manoj in Class 10. I'll tell you what happened, though I don't really know what goes on in his head. Over the holidays he watched a few videos about the Indus Valley script. Four or five, I think. He came back saying one video had "basically cracked it." In history class, when Pillai sir said nobody has deciphered the script yet, Manoj put up his hand. "Sir, that's outdated. It's been solved. I watched it." Sir asked, "By whom? Which symbols? How was it checked?" Manoj said, "The video explained it all," and looked annoyed. Sir didn't laugh. He said, "Bring the source, and let's look at it together on Friday." On Friday Manoj brought the video. It was one person's theory, and the comments were full of experts disagreeing. Manoj went quiet for the whole period.

qa.q: How many videos did Manoj watch about the Indus Valley script?
qa.a: Four or five.

qa.q: Why might Manoj feel sure he knew more than Pillai sir?
qa.a: The video sounded confident and complete, and Manoj didn't know enough yet to see what was missing, like who checked the idea or whether experts agreed.

qa.q: What did Pillai sir choose to do instead of laughing, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked Manoj to bring the source and look at it together on Friday. Seeing the disagreement himself taught Manoj more than being mocked would.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel watching Manoj go quiet on Friday?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel a bit sorry for Manoj, and maybe a little relieved that sir handled it without embarrassing him in front of everyone.

grounding: A classmate describes a teenage boy who watched a few videos and claimed to know more than his history teacher, until they checked the source.

passage:
Monday. Darshan, fifteen, had watched French videos all weekend: greetings, café phrases, a funny one about verbs. In class he corrected Urmila ma'am's pronunciation of "croissant" and said, "Honestly, the videos teach it better." A few classmates giggled. Urmila ma'am just said, "Wonderful. Then you can help me on Thursday."
Thursday. She gave him a short paragraph to read aloud and translate: a letter from a French student about her village. Darshan got through "Bonjour" and stopped. Past tense verbs. Words he'd never seen. He tried twice and his ears went hot. "I didn't know it had all this," he mumbled.
The next Monday. He stayed after class. "Ma'am, I think the videos gave me the easy parts. I didn't even know what I didn't know." Urmila ma'am smiled. "That's the first real step. Want the grammar sheet?" He took two.

qa.q: Which word's pronunciation did Darshan correct?
qa.a: He corrected Urmila ma'am's pronunciation of "croissant."

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel he knew French better than his teacher on Monday?
qa.a: Darshan felt proud and confident, because a weekend of videos gave him easy phrases that felt like a lot. He didn't yet know enough to see how much grammar and vocabulary he was missing.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Darshan choose to do after it?
qa.a: Trying to read the paragraph on Thursday showed him the gaps. The next Monday he stayed after class, admitted it and took two grammar sheets.

qa.q: How might Urmila ma'am have felt when Darshan corrected her in front of the class?
qa.a: She may have felt a flicker of annoyance, but she stayed calm and found a way to let him discover the gaps himself.

grounding: A teenage boy thinks a weekend of videos makes him better at French than his teacher, until a reading task shows him what he's missing.
